overview: Albania declared independence in 1912 and developed national institutions amid international pressure and war. Occupation, communist rule and the transition of the early 1990s repeatedly changed the relationship between citizens and the state. Its cultural history also includes skilled photography, textile making and communal music that crossed these political divides.

periods.title: Building independent institutions
periods.summary: Following the declaration of independence, a national bank was established in 1925 and national currency followed in 1926. Diplomatic recognition and institution building developed over years.

periods.title: Wartime occupation
periods.summary: Italian forces occupied Albania in 1939. German occupation followed Italy’s surrender in 1943, putting Jewish refugees and those protecting them in danger.

periods.title: Communist government and state control
periods.summary: The postwar government nationalized banking and concentrated economic power in state institutions. Under Enver Hoxha, Albania also experienced severe diplomatic isolation.

periods.title: Political and institutional transition
periods.summary: Albania restored diplomatic relations with the United States in 1991. Banking reforms in the early 1990s separated central banking from commercial activities.

periods.title: Constitutional republic
periods.summary: The constitution approved in 1998 defines Albania as a parliamentary republic and protects political pluralism, religious freedom and minority rights.

sections.title: Photography as craft and a record of life

items.text: The Marubi studio in Shkodër grew from Pietro Marubbi’s nineteenth-century work into a family tradition continued by Kel and Gegë. Early wet-collodion images gave way to dry gelatin on glass. This was a local mastery of changing photographic methods, not an Albanian invention of photography.

The archive records births, weddings and funerals alongside political figures. Studio compositions were deliberately staged. Photographs reveal clothing, gestures and social relationships, while reflecting choices made by photographers and their subjects. They do not transparently represent an entire society.

The private Marubi studio closed in 1952, and Gegë worked with other photographers in a state cooperative. His family archive entered state custody in 1970, and he continued organizing it. The collection therefore preserves both a photographic tradition and evidence of how socialist policies transformed private creative work.

The Bank of Albania’s catalog identifies a 1926 note bearing both 5 lek and 1 frank ari as the first national banknote. Printed by Richter in Naples, it circulated only briefly. The object ties Albania’s new monetary institution to overseas printing skills and a currency expressed in related units.

A 1939 issue reused a 1926 banknote with an eagle stamped over Ahmet Zogu’s portrait. A 100-franga note issued in May 1940 carried Victor Emanuel III’s portrait in its watermark. These alterations show political authority changing on an everyday object.

The xhubleta worn by women and girls in northern highland communities has an undulating bell shape. Makers prepare shajak, cut and sew it, then add embroidered motifs. Its form and decoration once communicated social and economic standing as well as requiring knowledge passed between skilled makers.

UNESCO’s account links declining xhubleta use to changes under socialism in the 1960s. The garment was impractical for work in agricultural cooperatives, while collectivization reduced access to materials. Its inclusion on the urgent safeguarding list in 2022 recognized a living skill whose transmission had become vulnerable.

Iso-polyphonic singing combines a melody, countermelody and a supporting vocal drone. Tosk singers sustain the drone through staggered breathing; Lab performances can make it rhythmic and attach words to it. Songs accompany weddings, funerals and harvest celebrations. The coordination of voices is part of social participation as well as musical accomplishment.

A 1943 photograph preserved by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum connects Gavra Mandil with Refik Veseli. The Mandils were Jewish refugees from Yugoslavia; photographic work in Tirana brought the families together. When danger increased under German occupation, Veseli arranged refuge at his family’s home in Krujë, where the Mandils survived.

The House of Leaves museum preserves miniature cameras, recorders, microphone transmitters and official instructions for surveillance. Such equipment required purchasing, maintenance and trained operators. The collection shows technical expertise serving political repression under communism, rather than treating every technological development as a social benefit.

Another exhibit displays a telephone interception list from the Ministry of Internal Affairs archive. The museum explains that household telephone access in 1970s Tirana required special authorization and favored officials, their connections and certain essential services. A phone could offer practical advantages while also enabling the state to monitor private conversations.

The 1998 constitution provides for freely formed political parties and separates state powers. It also protects expression, religious choice and the cultural and language rights of minorities. These provisions record the republic’s declared civic framework; the text itself cannot demonstrate how completely those guarantees were realized in daily life.

ending.text: Albania continues as a state. Italian occupation interrupted its independence in 1939, and the communist system later gave way to political change in the early 1990s. These were transformations of rule, not the disappearance of Albanian society. The 1998 constitution established the framework of a parliamentary republic.
